lesson.title: Your school’s AI policy
lesson.subtitle: Principles your whole school can keep

video.title: Your school’s AI policy
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah Rahman — teacher educator, Bangladesh (main character)
Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: A school corridor, two classroom doors side by side. Through the left door, a sign on the board: a phone with a red cross. Through the right door, homework on the board with a chat bubble. A pupil stands between the doors, shrugging. Dr Farah watches, thoughtful.
scenes.animation: Camera pans from door to door; a question mark pops above the pupil (≤ 200 ms).
scenes.narration: In one school I support, a teacher bans chatbots, and the teacher next door sets homework with one. The pupils have no idea what the rule is.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and a yellow ‘AI’ track chip with the spark icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: write your school’s AI policy, together.

scenes.visual: Left: a printed list of app names (shown as grey bars) curling and fading like an old calendar page. Right: a short card of principles, standing firm while new app tiles fly past it.
scenes.animation: The list yellows and curls (1 s); new tiles fly past the principles card.
scenes.on_screen_text: Principles, not a list of apps
scenes.narration: A school AI policy shouldn’t be a list of allowed apps. Apps change every few months, and the list is out of date before it’s printed. Principles last: they guide decisions about any tool, new or old.

scenes.visual: A poster titled with the AI chip fills with the first three principles, each with its icon: a target (purpose), a teacher beside a pupil (people responsible), a lock (privacy).
scenes.animation: Each principle slides in as it is said.
scenes.narration: Start with seven principles. Purpose: AI is used only when it helps learning. People stay responsible: a teacher checks what AI makes, and AI never decides alone about a pupil. Privacy: no pupils’ names, marks, photos or voices go into public tools.

scenes.visual: The poster continues with four more principles: scales (fairness), an eye (openness), a checked task sheet (honest assessment), a shared phone between pupils (equal access).
scenes.animation: Each principle slides in as it is said.
scenes.narration: Fairness: check that tools work for all your pupils, in their languages. Openness: say when AI was used, staff and pupils alike. Honesty in assessment: every task says how much AI is allowed. And equal access: no pupil falls behind for having no phone or no data.

scenes.visual: A flow of four steps: teachers drafting at a staff-room table; pupils and parents giving views at a meeting and on a phone group; a one-page policy pinned up; a calendar with a yearly loop arrow.
scenes.animation: Nodes appear one by one, 300 ms apart, with arrows drawing between them.
scenes.narration: So a school AI policy is a short set of shared principles, written with the people it affects. Staff draft it, then ask pupils and parents, at a meeting or in the class WhatsApp group. Agree it, put it on one page, and review it every year.

scenes.visual: A village well under a tree. Families gather round and agree the rules, a hand raised for each. Then the season changes: the ground dries, and the same families meet again.
scenes.animation: Hands rise one by one; a quick wipe from green to dry season.
scenes.narration: It’s like the rules for a shared village well. They work because the families agreed them. When the season changes, they meet and change them.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah pops in beside the poster of principles, a marker in hand. Three answer cards drop in below her.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Why write principles, not a list of approved apps?

scenes.visual: The card ‘Apps change; principles still apply’ gets a blue check badge. A new app tile arrives and passes three gates: learning, privacy, every pupil.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); the tile moves gate to gate.
scenes.narration: Apps change, and principles still apply. When a new tool arrives, nobody rewrites the policy: they ask if it serves learning, protects privacy and works for every pupil.

scenes.visual: A committee round a table: two teachers, a parent and a pupil. A matrix on the board: criteria down the side with their weights, three reading apps across the top. Scores fill in, then totals.
scenes.animation: Weights appear first; then scores fill cell by cell; totals pop at the bottom.
scenes.narration: Choosing a reading app, for example? Use a weighted decision matrix, in the open. First the committee agrees the criteria, like learning, privacy, offline use and cost, and their weights. Then score each app, multiply by the weights and add up. Publish the scores, so everyone sees why one app won.

scenes.visual: A phone screen with the Decide with numbers lab: sliders for how much cost, learning, travel time and safety matter, and three bars for the museum, the farm and the science centre. Two bars are equal; a finger nudges the learning slider and the science centre bar pulls ahead.
scenes.animation: Bars grow (1 s); the learning slider moves one step; one bar lengthens.
scenes.narration: In the app, you’ll choose a class trip, weighing cost, learning, travel time and safety. With the starting weights, the museum and the science centre tie. Raise learning by one point, and the science centre wins. Small changes decide, so agree the weights openly.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor holds a scoring sheet, a little sheepish; his favourite app is circled. Two answer cards appear beside him.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. I scored three apps first, then picked weights that made my favourite win. Is that a fair decision?

scenes.visual: The ‘No — agree the weights first’ card gets the check badge, then the screen resolves into four points of a good policy.
scenes.animation: Points tick in, 250 ms apart; the takeaway bar slides up.
scenes.narration: No: agree the weights before scoring, or the matrix just dresses up a favourite. Remember: principles, not app lists; written with pupils, parents and staff; reviewed every year; and tools chosen in the open.

scenes.visual: A classroom. Groups of pupils write rules on strips of paper; the class votes with raised hands; a poster titled ‘Our class AI charter’ goes up on the wall with five rules. Dr Farah smiles beside it.
scenes.animation: Strips fly onto the board; hands rise; the poster slides up.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: a “Class AI charter”. In groups, pupils suggest rules for using AI in your class. Together, choose five, vote on the wording and put the charter up. Review it at the end of term.

checkpoints.prompt: Why write principles, not a list of approved apps?

options.text: Lists are too long to print

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — new tools arrive every few months. Principles tell people how to decide about any of them.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — principles don’t allow everything. They last when apps change, and help people decide about any new tool.

checkpoints.prompt: Mr Okafor chose the weights after scoring the apps. Is that fair?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — weights chosen after scoring can make any favourite win. Agree them first, in the open.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the sums can be right and the choice still unfair. Weights chosen after scoring can make any favourite win.
